## What this page is

This is a **proof-of-concept** for documenting the Python package
[`sportsdataverse-py`](https://py.sportsdataverse.org) with
[Quarto](https://quarto.org). The point it demonstrates is **build-time
executable code cells**: every Python block below is *actually run* when the
page is rendered (`quarto render`), and its output — including tidy
**polars** / **pandas** DataFrames rendered as HTML tables — is frozen into
the static page. No browser runtime, no serverless proxy, no "trust me, this
is what it returns": the reader sees the genuine output of `sportsdataverse`
against the live ESPN endpoints as of the render.

Compare this side-by-side with the Docusaurus site under `docs/` — see
[`README.md`](./README.md) in this folder for the full Quarto-vs-Docusaurus
write-up.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1. The package surface

First, import the package and confirm the per-sport namespaces are all
present. This is a stable, offline-safe call — it touches no network.

```{python}
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # silence the harmless numexpr/bottleneck UserWarning

import sportsdataverse as sdv

sports = ["nba", "wnba", "nfl", "mlb", "nhl", "mbb", "wbb", "cfb", "odds"]
present = [s for s in sports if hasattr(sdv, s)]
present
```

Every sport submodule resolves. Each one exposes an `espn_<sport>_*` family
of tidy-data loaders. For example, the NBA namespace ships these ESPN
endpoints (first dozen shown):

```{python}
import sportsdataverse.nba as nba

nba_espn = [fn for fn in dir(nba) if fn.startswith("espn_nba_")]
print(f"{len(nba_espn)} espn_nba_* callables; first 12:")
nba_espn[:12]
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2. A real loader → a real DataFrame

Now the headline feature. We call `espn_nba_teams()` — a stable ESPN teams
endpoint — and let Quarto render the returned **polars** DataFrame as an HTML
table. This is *live data captured at build time*, not a hand-maintained
sample that drifts out of date.

```{python}
from sportsdataverse.nba import espn_nba_teams

teams = espn_nba_teams()        # -> polars.DataFrame
teams.shape                     # (rows, cols)
```

The frame is wide (logos, colors, slugs, uids…). Let's select the three
columns most readers care about and show the first ten teams. Quarto renders
the polars frame inline:

```{python}
teams.select(["team_id", "team_abbreviation", "team_display_name"]).head(10)
```

Because the package is polars-first but pandas-friendly, the same loader can
hand back a **pandas** frame with `return_as_pandas=True` — useful when the
reader's downstream stack is pandas. Quarto renders pandas frames just as
happily (note the `df-print: paged` styling from `_quarto.yml`):

```{python}
teams_pd = espn_nba_teams(return_as_pandas=True)
teams_pd[["team_id", "team_abbreviation", "team_display_name"]].head(5)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3. A second sport, same one-liner shape

The cross-league surface is uniform: `espn_<sport>_teams()` returns the same
tidy shape for every league. Here is the NFL equivalent — 32 teams, rendered
the same way:

```{python}
from sportsdataverse.nfl import espn_nfl_teams

nfl_teams = espn_nfl_teams()
nfl_teams.select(["team_id", "team_abbreviation", "team_display_name"]).head(8)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4. Inline computed results in prose

Quarto also supports **inline executable expressions**, so a sentence can
quote a *computed* number rather than a copy-pasted one that goes stale.

```{python}
n_nba = espn_nba_teams().height
n_nfl = espn_nfl_teams().height
```

As of this render, `sportsdataverse` reports **`{python} n_nba` NBA teams**
and **`{python} n_nfl` NFL teams** from the ESPN teams endpoints — and those
two numbers were computed by Python while this page was being built, not
typed in by hand.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Takeaway

Every table and number on this page is the *real* output of `sportsdataverse`
code, executed once at build time and frozen into static HTML. There is no
client-side Python, no live API call when a reader loads the page, and no
manually maintained "expected output" that can silently rot. That is the core
value proposition of Quarto for the SportsDataverse **Python** (and **R**)
data packages.

See [`README.md`](./README.md) for how this stacks up against the Docusaurus
toolchain the SportsDataverse uses elsewhere.
